Chapter One: The Unspoken Truths Behind Everyday Advice
You know, there’s a comfort in reading advice columns or tuning in to someone talk through life’s big questions. The words usually sound so polished, don’t they? The answers seem neat, as if every problem could be wrapped up with a tidy bow. But if you look a little closer, there’s a whole world underneath—full of hesitation, second-guessing, and all the things that never get said out loud.
Most folks don’t realize just how much is left out—how much of the real story never makes it onto the page or into the microphone. Imagine someone sitting at their kitchen table, pen in hand, staring at a blank sheet. The question in front of them feels simple: “How do I handle disappointment?” Eventually, sure, they write something practical, maybe even wise. But what you don’t see are the memories of their own recent letdowns, the sting of a friend’s broken promise, or those quiet tears on the drive home. The advice is true, but it just skims the surface. Underneath, there’s a silent confession: sometimes, the person giving advice is still figuring it out, too.
This is the tension running through so many public conversations. The person with the platform—the one holding the microphone or signing their name to the column—is supposed to have it all together. But behind the scenes, there’s a private world of doubts, fears, and unfinished thoughts. The gap between what’s said and what’s really felt? It can be huge. It’s easy to forget that the person offering guidance is just as human as anyone else.
And after the column is published, or the podcast goes live, there’s often this lingering feeling—“I wish I’d said more.” Not because the advice was wrong, but because it was incomplete. There’s this longing to share the messy parts—the moments of weakness, those whispered prayers in the dark, the times when faith feels thin and answers seem so far away.
Picture this: one evening, a woman sits with her phone, scrolling through messages from people who just read her latest piece. Some thank her for her honesty, others ask for more details, a few share their own struggles. She feels grateful... and a little exposed. And that’s the thing—real connection doesn’t happen when everything looks perfect. It happens when someone’s brave enough to be vulnerable.
Most people crave this kind of honesty. We want to know we’re not the only ones feeling confused or hurting. We want to hear that even the people who seem wise and put-together have battles of their own. There’s a quiet power in admitting, “I don’t have all the answers.” It opens the door for real conversation, for grace, for growth.
Faith, in these moments, isn’t about having the perfect response. It’s about showing up with authenticity. It’s trusting that God’s grace is big enough to fill the gaps, to cover the places where words just aren’t enough. The real work? It happens not in the polished advice, but in being willing to confess what’s actually going on inside.
Over time, you start to see that the deepest connections are built on honesty. The advice that sticks isn’t always the most eloquent—it’s the most real. When someone opens up about their struggles, their doubts, their hopes, it creates space for others to do the same. Once the unspoken truths are brought into the light, they have a way of healing—not just the person who shares them, but everyone who listens.
